Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].
citations.use_explanation: [F2] Independence of the generated sigma-algebras gives the product formula for every measurable rectangle in a finite product of real lines. The inverse image of each such rectangle under the coordinate tuple is a finite intersection of coordinate preimages, hence measurable; since the rectangles generate the finite product sigma-algebra, the tuple is a random element there. Iterating the sigma-finite product-measure theorem gives the finite product law of the marginals. It and the joint law agree on the generating pi-system of elementary rectangles, which contains the whole space with mass one, so the measure-uniqueness theorem identifies these laws. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $r_0=0$, nonnegativity of the finite sum implies every $r_j=0$, so the set of active clocks is empty and no finite candidate time is defined.

Suppose $r_0>0$. For $t\ge0$, independence in [F2] and the unit exponential survival in [F1] give $\mathbb P(T_*>t)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}\mathbb P(E_j>r_jt)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}e^{-r_jt}=e^{-r_0t}.$ Thus $T_*$ has the unique law $\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$ specified in [F1].

For a channel $j$ with $r_j>0$, the scaled clock $E_j/r_j$ has density $r_j e^{-r_jt}$ on $t>0$ by change of variables in [F1]. Independence [F2] therefore gives the joint density that channel $j$ rings first at time $t$ as $r_j e^{-r_jt}\prod_{k\ne j:r_k>0}e^{-r_kt}=r_j e^{-r_0t}.$ Integrating over $t>0$ yields $\mathbb P(J_*=j)=r_j/r_0$, and this joint density factors as $r_0e^{-r_0t}(r_j/r_0)$, proving independence of $T_*$ and $J_*$.

For distinct active $i,j$, the independent scaled clocks have continuous densities, so their equality has probability zero: conditioning on $E_i/r_i$ leaves the independent variable $E_j/r_j$ with zero probability at each singleton. A finite union over pairs shows the minimum is unique almost surely. Together with steps 1.2 and 2.1 this proves all assertions.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a finite measure space and let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be
measurable complex-valued functions with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. If
$|f_n|\le M$ almost everywhere for one real $M\ge0$, then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$.

Stop the process at $\tau_n:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\notin K_n\}$. The stopped path takes values in the finite set $F_n$ and is frozen after exit. Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. Conditional on the reaction history through time $s$, partition on the finite vector of last-used stream indices; on each part [F3] gives independence of all unused coordinates. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. The probability of at least two events within $h$ is at most $(M_nh)^2/2$ by integrating the summed first-two-event density, bounded by $M_n^2$, over the ordered two-time simplex. Since $V\le C_n$ on $F_n$, the first-event term differs from $h(QV)(x)$ by at most $C_nM_n^2h^2/2$, using $|1-e^{-z}|\le z$ for $z\ge0$; the multiple-event remainder is bounded by $2C_n(M_nh)^2/2$. Thus, uniformly over $x\in K_n$, the conditional mean increment is $h\,1_{\{s<\tau_n\}}(QV)(X_s)+O(h^2)$. This conditional mean is the explicit kernel average from the independent stream and survival ratio just computed; integrating it over finite reaction histories gives the unconditional mean increment. Sum those means on a uniform partition of $[0,t]$ and let the mesh tend to zero to obtain $\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]=V(x_0)+\mathbb E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}(QV)(X_s)\,ds.$ The error sum is $O(th)$; the pathwise Riemann sums converge by step 1.1 and are bounded by $t\max_{x\in K_n}|QV(x)|$, so [F5] passes their expectations to the limit. The same bounded Riemann-sum argument interchanges time integration and expectation for this bounded stopped integrand.

Set $g_n(t)=\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]$. From step 2.1, $QV\le cV$, and $V\ge1$, we obtain $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)+c\int_0^t g_n(s)\,ds.$ Here $g_n$ is bounded on each finite interval because $X_{t\wedge\tau_n}\in F_n$. Iterating the integral inequality $m$ times bounds it by $V(x_0)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(ct)^k/k!+C_n(ct)^m/m!$; the last term tends to zero and the sum tends to $V(x_0)e^{ct}$. Hence $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)e^{ct}$.
On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$ the exit state satisfies $V(X_{\tau_n})>n$, so $n\,\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le g_n(T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}$.

Fix any finite $T>0$. If $\tau_\infty\le T$ but $\tau_n>T$ for some integer $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$, infinitely many events occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$, an event of probability zero by step 1.1. A countable union over such $n$ is still null, so outside it explosion by $T$ forces $\tau_n\le T$ for every sufficiently large integer $n$. Step 4.1 gives $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty\le T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}/n$ for arbitrarily large $n$, hence this probability is zero. Taking integer $T\ge1$ proves $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. The argument uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice only as declared in [A1] and [A2]; it uses no Axiom of Choice.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.
citations.use_explanation: [F1] The reaction network specifies admissible increments, finite channel rates, and the time-dependent rate sum $\lambda(t,x)$. ([[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]])

**Inputs.** A finite or countable state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, finitely many time-dependent propensities $a_j(t,x)$ from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], a finite horizon $T>0$, initial state $x_0$, optional candidate budget $B\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ defaulting to $\infty$ (where $\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$), and a deterministic envelope $\Lambda<\infty$ with an admissibility certificate establishing
$$0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda\qquad(0\le t\le T, x\in E).$$
The global inequality is a precondition; the procedure does not verify the certificate exhaustively.
The random source supplies independent $E_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $U_n\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ sequences. Their countable product model uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; the unit exponential law and normalized unit-interval Lebesgue law are as in [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]].

**Procedure.** Set $t=0$, $x=x_0$, and candidate counter $n=0$. If $\Lambda=0$, return the constant path through $T$ with status absorbed. Otherwise, while $t<T$:

1. If $n=B$, return the path prefix with status budget-exhausted.
2. Set $\tau=E_{n+1}/\Lambda$. If $t+\tau\ge T$, return the state held through $T$ with status horizon.
3. Set $t\leftarrow t+\tau$ and evaluate $\lambda(t,x)$. If $\lambda(t,x)>\Lambda$ at this candidate, stop with status invalid-envelope; this pointwise runtime check detects only violations at candidate times and states that are actually evaluated. The algorithm does not continue by clipping the rate.
4. If $U_{n+1}\ge\lambda(t,x)/\Lambda$, reject this candidate and leave $x$ unchanged; set $n\leftarrow n+1$ and continue. Otherwise choose the first $J$ such that
$$U_{n+1}\Lambda<\sum_{j=1}^J a_j(t,x),$$
set $x\leftarrow x+\nu_J$, append the marked event $(t,J,x)$, set $n\leftarrow n+1$, and continue.

A time-dependent propensity without a certified finite envelope is outside this algorithm; integrated-hazard inversion is a separate method and is not used here. If the loop reaches $t=T$, return status horizon. If the global precondition is false, the procedure need not detect that failure: status invalid-envelope is returned only when the pointwise check in step 3 encounters a violation. No path law is claimed under a false global envelope.
citations.use_explanation: [F2] The global envelope is an admissibility precondition for the algorithm. Its pointwise runtime guard reports `invalid-envelope` only if it encounters a candidate time and state where $\lambda(t,x)>\Lambda$; it does not verify a global certificate exhaustively. ([[alg-dominating-thinning-for-time-varying-reaction-rates]])

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

Let $\nu$ be a finite Borel measure on $S$
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and put $\lambda=\nu(S)$. A
Poisson point process of intensity $\nu$ exists. If $\lambda=0$ it is the zero
process. If $\lambda>0$, its law is the push-forward of
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\left(\frac{\nu}{\lambda}\right)^{\otimes n}$$
on the disjoint union $\coprod_{n\ge0}S^n$ under
$(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. Every Poisson point
process of finite total intensity has this same law. This is the
**mixed-binomial representation**: the total count is Poisson and, in the
construction, the $n$ locations in component $S^n$ have product law
$(\nu/\lambda)^{\otimes n}$.
citations.use_explanation: [F5] Conditional on its Poisson total count, the finite-intensity candidate process has the normalized product intensity law, identifying the marked candidate pattern.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
citations.use_explanation: [A1] Countable Choice is used in the exponential and unit-interval probability laws. ([[def-countable-choice]])

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: First assume $\Lambda>0$. If the candidate interarrival increments are $E_n/\Lambda$, then for exactly $m$ candidates at ordered times $0<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le T$, the product of the $m$ exponential gap densities and the final no-candidate survival factor is $\prod_{i=1}^m\Lambda e^{-\Lambda(s_i-s_{i-1})}\cdot e^{-\Lambda(T-s_m)}=e^{-\Lambda T}\Lambda^m,$ where $s_0=0$. This is the ordered-event density in [F4]. The independent uniform marks give the conditional product-uniform mark law, so [F5] identifies the finite marked candidate pattern with a Poisson point process of intensity $\Lambda\,ds\,du$ on $(0,T]\times[0,1]$. By the defining independent-count property in [F5], restrictions to disjoint time intervals are independent; after translating time, the restriction to any interval of length $v$ has ordered-time density $e^{-\Lambda v}\Lambda^m$. In particular $N^*(T)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\Lambda T)$.

Fix deterministic $t$, condition on $\mathcal F_t$ with $X_t=x$, and let $0\le u\le T-t$. By step 1.1 and [F5], future candidates in $(t,t+u]\times[0,1]$ are independent of $\mathcal F_t$ and their ordered-time density is $e^{-\Lambda u}\Lambda^m$. For $s\in(t,t+u]$ put $b(s)=\Lambda-\lambda(s,x)\ge0$. Conditional on $m$ ordered candidate times, the probability all marks are rejected is the product of their rejection fractions. Using that density and Tonelli [F6], the conditional probability of no accepted candidate is $e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\int_{t<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le t+u}\prod_{i=1}^m b(s_i)\,ds_1\cdots ds_m =e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{(\int_t^{t+u}b(s)\,ds)^m}{m!} =e^{-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds}.$ The middle identity holds because the symmetric product integrand has equal integrals on the $m!$ orderings of the cube; ties form a Lebesgue-null set.

Fix a channel $j$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq(t,T]$. By step 1.1 and [F5], future candidate points on $(t,T]$ are independent of $\mathcal F_t$ and have ordered-time density $e^{-\Lambda(T-t)}\Lambda^m$. For the first accepted candidate to occur at time $s\in B$ with mark in $D_j(s,x)$, all earlier candidates must be rejected, its mark must lie in a set of measure $a_j(s,x)/\Lambda$, and later candidates are unrestricted. For $k$ earlier rejected candidates, integration over their ordered times contributes $(\int_t^s b(v)\,dv)^k/k!$; for $\ell$ later unrestricted candidates, integration contributes $(\Lambda(T-s))^\ell/\ell!$. Summing the nonnegative series and using [F6], the first-event measure on $B$ is $e^{-\Lambda(T-t)}\int_B a_j(s,x)\left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(\int_t^s b(v)\,dv)^k}{k!}\right)\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\frac{(\Lambda(T-s))^\ell}{\ell!}\right)ds =\int_B a_j(s,x)e^{-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv}\,ds.$ This proves the channel-specific first-event law for arbitrary Borel rates and for disjoint mark sets of the specified measures whose time-mark regions are product-measurable; their locations within $[0,1]$ do not enter the calculation. The endpoint mark conventions differ only on a null set.

At an accepted candidate time the new state depends only on the past and that candidate's time and mark. If its candidate index is $K$, the event $\{K=n\}$ is determined by the first $n$ gap and mark coordinates; partitioning over finite $n$ shows that the coordinates after $K$ retain their prescribed product law. Thus the same two calculations restart at the new state and time. Since $N(T)\le N^*(T)$ pathwise, [F7] and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$ and $N(T)<\infty$ almost surely. If the global envelope hypothesis is false, this theorem asserts no path law; the algorithm returns `invalid-envelope` only if its pointwise guard encounters a violating candidate as specified in [F2]. Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 establish the candidate law, both conditional event laws, the restart rule and the finite-count bound under the global envelope.

citations.quote:
Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $R\ge1$, let $r_1,\ldots,r_R\ge0$, and set $r_0=\sum_{j=1}^R r_j$. On a common probability space let $E_1,\ldots,E_R$ be independent random variables, each with the unit exponential law $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, whose survival at $t\ge0$ is $e^{-t}$. If $r_0>0$, define
$$T_*:=\min_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j},\qquad J_*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j}.$$
Then ties have probability zero, $T_*\sim\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$, $J_*$ is independent of $T_*$, and
$$\mathbb P(J_*=j)=\frac{r_j}{r_0}.$$
If $r_0=0$, every $r_j=0$ and no finite reaction clock is active.

**Inputs.** A finite state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, a finite-channel reaction propensity system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], an initial state $x_0\in E$, a horizon $T>0$, and an optional event budget $B\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, defaulting to $\infty$, where $\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The random source is a sequence $(E_n,U_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $E_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $U_n$ uniform on $[0,1]$, all coordinates mutually independent. The countable product construction for these input laws uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice by [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]]; the exponential law uses Countable Choice by [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]]. For the uniform law, [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] makes the set function in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] a measure, and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] gives its restriction to $[0,1]$ mass one and interval probabilities equal to interval lengths.

**Procedure.** Set $t=0$, $x=x_0$, $n=0$, and record the initial state. While $t<T$:

1. Compute $\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$. If $\lambda(x)=0$, keep the state equal to $x$ through $T$ and return status absorbed.
2. If $n=B$, return the path prefix through $(t,x)$ with status budget-exhausted; this status does not assert that the horizon was reached.
3. Set $\tau=E_{n+1}/\lambda(x)$. If $t+\tau\ge T$, keep the state equal to $x$ through $T$ and return status horizon.
4. Set $J$ to the least index with $U_{n+1}<\lambda(x)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^J a_j(x)$. If the null event $U_{n+1}=1$ occurs, use the largest index with $a_j(x)>0$. This rule never selects a zero-rate channel.
5. Set $t\leftarrow t+\tau$, $x\leftarrow x+\nu_J$, append the marked event $(t,J,x)$, and set $n\leftarrow n+1$.

If the loop reaches $t=T$, return the path through $T$ with status horizon. Each event uses a linear scan of the $R$ propensities and a linear cumulative channel search; no update-tree acceleration is part of this procedure. If $B<\infty$ and the budget expires before $T$, the returned prefix is incomplete.

The procedure assumes an ideal independent random source with the displayed laws. It makes no claim that a finite-state pseudorandom generator supplies independent exact exponential or uniform variables.

**Inputs.** A finite state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, a finite-channel time-homogeneous system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], initial state $x_0\in E$, horizon $T>0$, and optional reaction-event budget $B\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, defaulting to $\infty$, where $\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Supply independent unit exponential increments $E_{j,k}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ for $1\le j\le R$ and $k\ge1$. The countable product construction uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice by [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]]; the exponential law assumes Countable Choice by [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]].

**Initialization.** Set $t=0$, $x=x_0$, $n=0$, internal times $A_j=0$, threshold indices $m_j=1$, and next thresholds $S_j=E_{j,1}$ for each channel.

**Procedure.** At each state $x$:

1. Compute $a_j(x)$ for every channel. If $\lambda(x)=0$, return the constant path through $T$ with status absorbed.
2. If $n=B$, return the path prefix with status budget-exhausted. For each $j$, set $\Delta_j=(S_j-A_j)/a_j(x)$ when $a_j(x)>0$ and $\Delta_j=+\infty$ when $a_j(x)=0$.
3. Let $\Delta=\min_j\Delta_j$. If $t+\Delta>T$, return the path held at $x$ through $T$ with status horizon.
4. Let $J$ be the least minimizing channel (ties have probability zero). For every channel set $A_j\leftarrow A_j+a_j(x)\Delta$. Set $t\leftarrow t+\Delta$, $x\leftarrow x+\nu_J$, append the marked event, then set $m_J\leftarrow m_J+1$ and $S_J\leftarrow S_J+E_{J,m_J}$; finally set $n\leftarrow n+1$.

On the returned time interval (through $T$ unless the budget is exhausted), the internal time is $A_j(t)=\int_0^t a_j(X_{s-})\,ds$, and almost surely the random-time-change representation is
$$X_t=X_0+\sum_{j=1}^R\nu_jY_j(A_j(t)),$$
where $S_{j,k}=\sum_{q=1}^k E_{j,q}$ and $Y_j(u)=\#\{k:S_{j,k}\le u\}$. An event at exactly $T$ is recorded before returning. If the loop reaches $t=T$, return the path through $T$ with status horizon. With unlimited budget, [[thm-finite-state-gillespie-and-next-reaction-exactness]] proves the Poisson threshold-clock laws and equality with the direct method's reaction path law. The implementation scans all $R$ channels at each event; no logarithmic update-tree cost is claimed.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be finite or countable, with finitely many time-dependent propensities $a_j(t,x)$ on $[0,T]$ as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Suppose a certified constant envelope $0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda<\infty$ holds for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in E$. Then the dominating-thinning algorithm in [[alg-dominating-thinning-for-time-varying-reaction-rates]], with an unlimited candidate budget, has the following exact conditional law from time $t$ and state $x$:

Write $\mathcal F_t$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the candidate times and marks in $(0,t]$. Then, for $0\le t\le T$, $x\in E$, and $0\le u\le T-t$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{no accepted reaction in }(t,t+u]\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds\right),\qquad 0\le u\le T-t,$$

and for every Borel $B\subseteq(t,T]$ and channel $j$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{first accepted reaction time lies in }B,\ J=j\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\int_B a_j(s,x)\exp\!\left(-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv\right)ds.$$

After a reaction, the same rule restarts at its new time and state. Candidate events on $[0,T]$ have a Poisson count of mean $\Lambda T$; accepted reactions are a subset, so there are finitely many accepted reactions almost surely and $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$. The conclusion is conditional on the stated envelope; no law is asserted when it fails.

When $\Lambda>0$, the same two conditional-law conclusions hold if, at each fixed $(s,x)$, channel $j$ is accepted on a Borel mark set $D_j(s,x)\subseteq[0,1]$, provided these sets are pairwise disjoint, have Lebesgue measure $a_j(s,x)/\Lambda$, and for each fixed state $x$ the region
$$\{(s,u)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]:u\in D_j(s,x)\}$$
is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$. The standard cumulative intervals in the algorithm are one such choice: their endpoints are finite sums of the Borel time sections $a_k(\cdot,x)/\Lambda$, so their time-mark regions are product-measurable. If $\Lambda=0$, the step 5.1 constant-path case applies. This equivalent mark-set form is used by the minimum-intensity coupling construction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: For one channel clock sequence with independent unit exponential gaps, the joint density of exactly $m$ ordered thresholds $0<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le u$ and no next threshold by $u$ is $\prod_{i=1}^m e^{-(s_i-s_{i-1})}\,e^{-(u-s_m)}=e^{-u},\qquad s_0=0.$ This agrees with [F4] at unit rate, so each $Y_j$ in the next-reaction construction is a unit-rate Poisson process on finite windows. The streams for distinct channels are independent by [F5], and after an event the unused sequence coordinates remain independent: partition on the finite index of the last used coordinate and use the finite-coordinate product law.

At state $x$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, the direct method's waiting time $E/\lambda(x)$ has survival $e^{-\lambda(x)t}$ by [F2]. The disjoint cumulative intervals for $U$ have lengths $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$, so channel $j$ is selected with that probability; because $U$ and $E$ are independent, the channel is independent of the waiting time. Thus the direct method uses exactly the reference event kernel. If $\lambda(x)=0$, it returns the absorbing path specified in the Statement.

At a state $x$, the next-reaction clock of channel $j$ has residual internal threshold distributed as an independent $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ variable. By [F2] their minimum has the same event-time and channel law as in step 1.2. After a reaction at elapsed time $\delta$, every nonwinning channel $k$ is conditioned only on its threshold exceeding $a_k(x)\delta$; memorylessness follows exactly from $\mathbb P(E_k>a_k(x)\delta+u\mid E_k>a_k(x)\delta)=e^{-u}.$ The residual thresholds remain independent because the conditioning events factor across independent clocks, and the fired channel receives a fresh independent exponential increment. Induction over the reaction count proves that every successive event kernel agrees with step 1.2, hence the full marked path law agrees. The threshold construction also gives $X_t=X_0+\sum_j\nu_jY_j(\int_0^t a_j(X_{s-})ds)$ by its definition.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

**Inputs.** Two finite-state reaction systems $X$ and $Y$ with the same finite channel labels $j=1,\ldots,R$. Their state sets may differ, and channel $j$ has respective increments $\nu_j^X,\nu_j^Y$ and propensities $a_j^X(x),a_j^Y(y)$ as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Supply an initial pair $(x_0,y_0)$, a horizon $T>0$, and an optional candidate budget $B\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, defaulting to $\infty$, where $\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.

For each channel set
$$M_j:=\max\left\{\max_{x\in E_X}a_j^X(x),\max_{y\in E_Y}a_j^Y(y)\right\},\qquad M:=\sum_{j=1}^R M_j.$$
These are finite because both state sets are finite. Supply mutually independent $E_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $U_n\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ for $n\ge1$. The countable input product uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; the exponential and uniform laws are those of [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]].

**Procedure.** Set $t=0$, $(x,y)=(x_0,y_0)$, and $n=0$. If $M=0$, return the two constant paths through $T$ with status absorbed. Otherwise define fixed mark blocks $I_j=[b_{j-1},b_j)$, where $b_0=0$ and $b_j=M^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^jM_k$; omit empty blocks when $M_j=0$, and include the endpoint $1$ in the last nonempty block. 1. If $n=B$, return the pair of path prefixes with status budget-exhausted.
2. Set $\tau=E_{n+1}/M$. If $t+\tau\ge T$, return both paths held through $T$ with status horizon.
3. Set $t\leftarrow t+\tau$. Find the unique nonempty block $I_j$ containing $U_{n+1}$ and set $v=(U_{n+1}-b_{j-1})/(M_j/M)$. Fire channel $j$ in $X$ if $v<a_j^X(x)/M_j$, and fire it in $Y$ if $v<a_j^Y(y)/M_j$. If both fire, record a shared event and update both states; if only one fires, record its residual event and update only that state; if neither fires, reject the candidate and leave both states fixed. Increment $n$ once for every candidate, including a rejected candidate. Endpoint marks have probability zero, so the last-block convention at $U_{n+1}=1$ does not affect the path law.

The candidate mark block for channel $j$ has length $M_j/M$. Within it the two acceptance intervals start at the same endpoint and have respective lengths $a_j^X(x)/M$ and $a_j^Y(y)/M$. Thus their overlap has candidate intensity $\min(a_j^X(x),a_j^Y(y))$, and the two residual portions have intensities $(a_j^X(x)-a_j^Y(y))_+$ and $(a_j^Y(y)-a_j^X(x))_+$. Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be finite or countable, with finitely many time-dependent propensities $a_j(t,x)$ on $[0,T]$ as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Suppose a certified constant envelope $0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda<\infty$ holds for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in E$. Then the dominating-thinning algorithm in [[alg-dominating-thinning-for-time-varying-reaction-rates]], with an unlimited candidate budget, has the following exact conditional law from time $t$ and state $x$:

Write $\mathcal F_t$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the candidate times and marks in $(0,t]$. Then, for $0\le t\le T$, $x\in E$, and $0\le u\le T-t$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{no accepted reaction in }(t,t+u]\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds\right),\qquad 0\le u\le T-t,$$

and for every Borel $B\subseteq(t,T]$ and channel $j$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{first accepted reaction time lies in }B,\ J=j\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\int_B a_j(s,x)\exp\!\left(-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv\right)ds.$$

After a reaction, the same rule restarts at its new time and state. Candidate events on $[0,T]$ have a Poisson count of mean $\Lambda T$; accepted reactions are a subset, so there are finitely many accepted reactions almost surely and $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$. $$\{(s,u)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]:u\in D_j(s,x)\}$$
is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$. The standard cumulative intervals in the algorithm are one such choice: their endpoints are finite sums of the Borel time sections $a_k(\cdot,x)/\Lambda$, so their time-mark regions are product-measurable. If $\Lambda=0$, the step 5.1 constant-path case applies. This equivalent mark-set form is used by the minimum-intensity coupling construction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Write $\mathcal F_t$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the candidate times and marks in $(0,t]$. Then, for $0\le t\le T$, $x\in E$, and $0\le u\le T-t$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{no accepted reaction in }(t,t+u]\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds\right),\qquad 0\le u\le T-t,$$

and for every Borel $B\subseteq(t,T]$ and channel $j$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{first accepted reaction time lies in }B,\ J=j\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\int_B a_j(s,x)\exp\!\left(-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv\right)ds.$$

After a reaction, the same rule restarts at its new time and state. Candidate events on $[0,T]$ have a Poisson count of mean $\Lambda T$; accepted reactions are a subset, so there are finitely many accepted reactions almost surely and $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$. The conclusion is conditional on the stated envelope; no law is asserted when it fails.

When $\Lambda>0$, the same two conditional-law conclusions hold if, at each fixed $(s,x)$, channel $j$ is accepted on a Borel mark set $D_j(s,x)\subseteq[0,1]$, provided these sets are pairwise disjoint, have Lebesgue measure $a_j(s,x)/\Lambda$, and for each fixed state $x$ the region
$$\{(s,u)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]:u\in D_j(s,x)\}$$
is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$. The standard cumulative intervals in the algorithm are one such choice: their endpoints are finite sums of the Borel time sections $a_k(\cdot,x)/\Lambda$, so their time-mark regions are product-measurable. If $\Lambda=0$, the step 5.1 constant-path case applies. This equivalent mark-set form is used by the minimum-intensity coupling construction.

$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$

$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$

$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, a **continuous-time filtration** is a family
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ such that
$\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ whenever $0\le s\le t$. A process
$X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** when $X_t$ is measurable from
$(\Omega,\mathcal F_t)$ to its state space at every $t$.

For any process of random elements $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$, its **natural
filtration** is

$$\mathcal F_t^X=\sigma\!\left(\{X_u^{-1}(C):0\le u\le t,\ C\text{ measurable in the state space of }X_u\}\right).$$

The generated sigma-algebra exists by
[[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]]. Its generator families
are nested in $t$, so $(\mathcal F_t^X)_{t\ge0}$ is a filtration; every
$X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t^X$-measurable, and minimality makes this the smallest
filtration to which $X$ is adapted. No completion or right-continuous
augmentation is included.

A real process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **all-pairs continuous-time
martingale** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when:

1. $M$ is adapted;
2. $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$; and
3. for every $0\le s\le t$,
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$

The equality in clause 3 is equality of the almost-everywhere classes in
[[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]. At $s=t$ it is the
known-variable identity. The word “continuous-time” specifies the index set;
it does not assert path continuity. Likewise the definition imposes neither
right continuity nor completeness on the filtration. AC is declared exactly
because the library's conditional-expectation existence theorem uses it; the
filtration, adaptation, and natural-filtration constructions make no choices.

filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with

contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.
