Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal G_t$ be generated by candidate times and marks up to $t$; these sigma-algebras increase with $t$, so [F5] makes them a continuous-time filtration. If $\Lambda=0$, all rates and all counts vanish. Otherwise the thinning realization has a rate-$\Lambda$ candidate process, and [F2] gives the same reaction path law as Gillespie. By [F3], candidates have no ties and their number on $[0,T]$ is finite almost surely. Hence each $N_j$ is adapted, nondecreasing and integer-valued with unit jumps and finite terminal value; also $N_j(T)\le N^*(T)$ and $0\le A_j(T)\le\Lambda T$. The state path is piecewise constant with finitely many jumps. Its left-limit process $X_{s-}$ is a pointwise limit of left-grid processes taking the value $X_{k2^{-n}}$ on $(k2^{-n},(k+1)2^{-n}]$; each is measurable for the generators in [F4]. Thus $a_j(X_{s-})$ is predictable. Because the density is bounded and piecewise constant along the path, for fixed $t$ its time integral is the limit of left-grid Riemann sums of values known by time $t$, so $A_j(t)$ is $\mathcal G_t$-measurable. The integral is continuous and bounded by $\Lambda T$; continuous adapted processes are pointwise limits of their left-grid predictable approximations, so $A_j$ is predictable with finite mean.

Fix deterministic $s$ and $0<h\le T-s$, and condition on $\mathcal G_s$ with $X_s=x$. The first accepted channel-$j$ event has density $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$ at elapsed time $u$, by [F2]. Its probability over $0<u\le h$ differs from $a_j(x)h$ by at most $a_j(x)\lambda(x)h^2/2\le\Lambda^2h^2/2$. Further channel-$j$ events require at least two candidates; if $N^*$ is their count and $\mu=\Lambda h$, then [F3] gives $\mathbb E(N^*1_{\{N^*\ge2\}})=\mu(1-e^{-\mu})\le\mu^2$. Therefore $\left|\mathbb E(N_j(s+h)-N_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)-a_j(x)h\right|\le\tfrac32\Lambda^2h^2.$ If no candidate occurs in $(s,s+h]$, the state stays at $x$ and the compensator increment equals $a_j(x)h$. Otherwise both that increment and $a_j(x)h$ lie between $0$ and $\Lambda h$, while the conditional probability of a candidate is at most $\Lambda h$. Therefore $\left|\mathbb E(A_j(s+h)-A_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)-a_j(x)h\right|\le\Lambda^2h^2,$ so $|\mathbb E(M_j(s+h)-M_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)|\le\tfrac52\Lambda^2h^2$. For $B\in\mathcal G_s$, partition $[s,t]$ into intervals of mesh at most $\delta$; conditional expectation on each left endpoint bounds $|\mathbb E(1_B(M_j(t)-M_j(s)))|$ by $\tfrac52\Lambda^2\delta(t-s)$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives zero for every $B\in\mathcal G_s$, which is the all-pairs martingale identity. Since $N_j(T)\le N^*(T)$ and $A_j(T)\le\Lambda T$, the bound $M_j(T)^2\le2N_j(T)^2+2A_j(T)^2$ and [F3] give $\mathbb E M_j(T)^2<\infty$; the same bound applies at every $t\le T$. Thus $M_j$ is square-integrable.

Candidates are simple, and each candidate mark selects at most one reaction channel. Therefore no two distinct channel counts jump together. Steps 1.1–2.1 verify the simple-count, finite-mean continuous predictable compensator, and square-integrable martingale hypotheses of [F6]. Applying [F7] gives $[M_j]=N_j$ and $\langle M_j\rangle=A_j$; applying [F8] to each distinct pair gives $[M_i,M_j]=\langle M_i,M_j\rangle=0$.

For bounded predictable step integrands $H_i,H_j$ on a common deterministic partition, expand $\mathbb E(I_iI_j)$, where $I_i=\int H_i\,dM_i$. Terms from distinct time intervals vanish by conditioning on the left endpoint of the later interval and using the martingale property from step 2.1. On an interval of length $h$, the same-interval product has conditional absolute expectation at most $5\Lambda^2h^2$: the product of distinct channel counts is zero unless at least two candidates occur, whose $N^{*2}$ expectation is $\mu^2+\mu(1-e^{-\mu})\le2\mu^2$; the two count-compensator terms are each at most $\Lambda h\,\mathbb E(N^*\mid\mathcal G_s)\le\Lambda^2h^2$, and the compensator product is at most $\Lambda^2h^2$. If the step coefficients are bounded in absolute value by $K$, multiplying by them gives a bound $5K^2\Lambda^2h^2$. Refining the common partition leaves each step integral unchanged and makes the sum of these bounds tend to zero, so $\mathbb E(I_iI_j)=0$.

For general $H_j$ in the stated finite-energy class, [F10] supplies bounded predictable step approximations in each compensator $L^2$ norm. By [F9], their individual integrals converge in $L^2$ to $I_j=\int_0^T H_j\,dM_j$ and satisfy $\mathbb E I_j^2=\mathbb E\int_0^T H_j^2\,dA_j$. For each $i\ne j$, use the linearity and modulus inequality in [F12], then apply [F11] to the expanded product difference, to obtain $|\mathbb E(I_i^{(n)}I_j^{(n)})-\mathbb E(I_iI_j)|\le\|I_i^{(n)}-I_i\|_2\|I_j^{(n)}\|_2+\|I_i\|_2\|I_j^{(n)}-I_j\|_2\to0$, since the isometry bounds the approximating norms. Step 3.2 therefore gives $\mathbb E(I_iI_j)=0$. Expanding the square of the finite sum now yields the displayed vector isometry because $dA_j=a_j(X_{s-})ds$. The proof uses AC only through [A1], the input-stream construction only through [A2]–[A3], and counts zero-increment reactions because they remain marked candidate acceptances.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be countable and let a finite-channel system be as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. For an initial state $x_0\in E$, construct its minimal reaction process recursively: at state $x$, wait an exponential time with parameter $\lambda(x)$, choose channel $j$ with probability $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$, and move to $x+\nu_j$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, remain at $x$ forever. Use an independent stream of these exponential and uniform random inputs, whose countable product law exists by Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For $V:E\to[1,\infty)$, call $V$ **proper** when $\{x:V(x)\le n\}$ is finite for every integer $n\ge1$. For this possibly unbounded $V$, define the finite local expression
$$(QV)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(V(x+\nu_j)-V(x)\bigr);$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, set $\Lambda:=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\lambda(x):x\in E\})<\infty$; thus $\Lambda=0$ for $E=\varnothing$ and $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ otherwise. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

$$0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda\qquad(0\le t\le T, x\in E).$$
The global inequality is a precondition; the procedure does not verify the certificate exhaustively.
The random source supplies independent $E_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $U_n\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ sequences. Their countable product model uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; the unit exponential law and normalized unit-interval Lebesgue law are as in [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]].

**Procedure.** Set $t=0$, $x=x_0$, and candidate counter $n=0$. If $\Lambda=0$, return the constant path through $T$ with status absorbed. Otherwise, while $t<T$:

1. If $n=B$, return the path prefix with status budget-exhausted.
2. Set $\tau=E_{n+1}/\Lambda$. If $t+\tau\ge T$, return the state held through $T$ with status horizon.
3. Set $t\leftarrow t+\tau$ and evaluate $\lambda(t,x)$. If $\lambda(t,x)>\Lambda$ at this candidate, stop with status invalid-envelope; this pointwise runtime check detects only violations at candidate times and states that are actually evaluated. The algorithm does not continue by clipping the rate.
4. If $U_{n+1}\ge\lambda(t,x)/\Lambda$, reject this candidate and leave $x$ unchanged; set $n\leftarrow n+1$ and continue. Otherwise choose the first $J$ such that
$$U_{n+1}\Lambda<\sum_{j=1}^J a_j(t,x),$$
set $x\leftarrow x+\nu_J$, append the marked event $(t,J,x)$, set $n\leftarrow n+1$, and continue.

A time-dependent propensity without a certified finite envelope is outside this algorithm; integrated-hazard inversion is a separate method and is not used here. If the loop reaches $t=T$, return status horizon. If the global precondition is false, the procedure need not detect that failure: status invalid-envelope is returned only when the pointwise check in step 3 encounters a violation. No path law is claimed under a false global envelope.

Suppose a certified constant envelope $0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda<\infty$ holds for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in E$. Then the dominating-thinning algorithm in [[alg-dominating-thinning-for-time-varying-reaction-rates]], with an unlimited candidate budget, has the following exact conditional law from time $t$ and state $x$:

Write $\mathcal F_t$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the candidate times and marks in $(0,t]$. Then, for $0\le t\le T$, $x\in E$, and $0\le u\le T-t$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{no accepted reaction in }(t,t+u]\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds\right),\qquad 0\le u\le T-t,$$

and for every Borel $B\subseteq(t,T]$ and channel $j$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{first accepted reaction time lies in }B,\ J=j\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\int_B a_j(s,x)\exp\!\left(-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv\right)ds.$$

After a reaction, the same rule restarts at its new time and state. Candidate events on $[0,T]$ have a Poisson count of mean $\Lambda T$; accepted reactions are a subset, so there are finitely many accepted reactions almost surely and $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$. $$\{(s,u)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]:u\in D_j(s,x)\}$$
is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$. **Inputs.** Two finite-state reaction systems $X$ and $Y$ with the same finite channel labels $j=1,\ldots,R$. Their state sets may differ, and channel $j$ has respective increments $\nu_j^X,\nu_j^Y$ and propensities $a_j^X(x),a_j^Y(y)$ as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]].
